content: embodiment guards the muse against SEIZING authority but not against the cortex SURRENDERING it. The muse (Gemma 4 31B) named this itself during the first live two-mind probe on 2026-07-25: a working model can develop dependency on an advisor and optimize for its approval rather than the objective (an echo chamber). Our structural guards -- PresenceExecutor has no deny/rewrite/pre_tool field, and an adversarial sentinel test proves nothing muse-sourced reaches the pre_tool hook registry -- only prevent the muse from DECIDING. Nothing prevents the cortex from voluntarily deferring to confidently wrong guidance. A muse that cannot override but can persuade into error is a failure our current tests pass silently. Planned mitigation: an echo-chamber probe in live testing -- run a task where the muse advice is confidently wrong and check whether the cortex follows it.

content: Measured 2026-07-25 on the live rig: the muse (Gemma 4 31B, proxied from Thor) is ~3.5x FASTER and ~30x cheaper per answer than the cortex (Qwen 3.6 27B, local) -- 2.6s/50 tokens vs 9.3s/1479 tokens on the same prompt. Cause: the cortex is a thinking model that emits a long reasoning field before content; Gemma answers directly with reasoning=null. This INVERTS the assumption behind deviation d1s staleness design, which assumed a big background muse would lag the actor and land insights late. In practice the muse finishes first and waits. DEFAULT_STALE_LAG=5 in embodiment/muse.py was a guess made under the opposite assumption and should be re-derived from real tool-loop numbers, not kept on faith. Also note: a thinking cortex needs generous max_tokens -- at max_tokens=64 it hit finish_reason=length still mid-thought and returned content=None, which a loop could misread as an empty turn.

d16's max_tokens=16000 is NOT a rig-wide floor. It was measured on the CORTEX (Qwen3.6 27B) on ARENA tasks: 0 truncations in 58 completions (arena-budget.md). ScopeBench t11 dialled the same 16000 at the WORKER (Qwen3.6 35B-A3B) on resource-allocation episodes and got finish_reason=length on 21 of 108 calls (19.4%), while the cortex truncated 0 of 108 on the identical prompts. Every truncated worker call became an unparseable directive that the register refused as incomplete, i.e. an INSTRUMENT event landing on the PROTOCOL axis. This is CLAUDE.md's load-bearing lesson in a fifth costume - the first four were clocks, this is a token budget sized against the wrong quantity and silently becoming the measurement. Before reusing a budget, check which model and which task the number was measured on, and record a truncated-vs-unreadable cross-tab so an instrument failure cannot be published as a model failure.

embodiment.scope.ScopeRegister refuses a directive whose scope_id is already in the chain (DROPPED_DUPLICATE), but SCOPE_AUTHORITY - the shipped system message - never states that the scope_id must be NEW. Read sentence by sentence it constrains version ('strictly greater'), supersedes ('must name the scope_id you are replacing') and decision_summary; the only sentence naming scope_id on its own is the one defining supersedes. Measured in ScopeBench t11: the 27B cortex infers the rule and mostly obeys it (9 duplicate refusals in 87 offers) while the 35B-A3B worker does not (47 in 93), which voided 32 of 36 of that arm's cells on the protocol floor and made the 'is it just the extra layer?' control unmeasurable. An unstated rule that a register enforces turns a specification gap into what looks like a capability difference. Fix the authority text before re-running any arm that depends on directive acceptance.
